content_units: Likely Non-Emergency Causes of New Knee Pain
Based on what you described, this pattern often fits a   non-emergency overuse or irritation problem  , especially after increasing walking.
Common general possibilities include:
-   Patellofemoral pain  : pain around or behind the kneecap, often worse with   stairs  , especially going downstairs.
-   Mild tendon or soft-tissue irritation  : the knee can get sore when activity increases faster than the joint is used to.
-   Early osteoarthritis flare  : common with age; may cause aching, stiffness, or pain with walking, stairs, or after sitting.
-   Pes anserine or other mild bursitis/tendon irritation  : can happen from repetitive walking, even without a clear injury.
-   Muscle weakness or tightness around the hip/thigh/calf  : this can change knee tracking and make stairs more painful.
What makes a dangerous cause less likely from your description:
-   No injury
-   No swelling
-   No fever
-   Still tied to activity  , especially stairs
When Knee Pain Needs Urgent Attention
Seek   urgent care or prompt medical evaluation   if any of these appear:
-   Sudden major swelling
-   Redness, warmth, or fever
-   Unable to bear weight   or the knee gives out repeatedly
-   Locked knee   that cannot fully bend or straighten
-   Severe calf pain/swelling  , especially one-sided
-   Chest pain or shortness of breath
-   Pain rapidly worsening   instead of gradually settling
-   Numbness, weakness, or major loss of function
-   Pain after a fall or twist   that was not initially obvious
Also arrange a   non-urgent clinician visit soon   if:
- pain lasts   more than 2-4 more weeks
- it keeps limiting stairs or walking
- morning stiffness becomes significant
- the knee starts swelling or catching
7-Day Low-Impact Home-Care Plan
This is a general, non-diagnostic plan aimed at calming irritation while keeping him gently active.
Day   Focus   Walking   Mobility/Strength   Symptom Relief
1   Reduce irritation   Cut walks to   10-15 min easy pace   on flat ground   Gentle knee bend/straighten 10 reps; ankle pumps 20 reps   Ice 15 min, 3-4 times
2   Protect stairs   Same or slightly less if sore   Seated leg raises 2 x 8 each side; gentle calf stretch   Ice after activity; elevate when resting
3   Light recovery   10-15 min flat walk only if pain stays mild   Sit-to-stand from chair 1-2 x 6; gentle hamstring stretch   Consider warm compress before movement, ice after
4   Recheck tolerance   Up to 15-20 min flat walk if improving   Quad tightening 2 x 10; side leg lifts 2 x 8   Keep stairs slow, use rail
5   Maintain low impact   Flat walk or stationary cycling with very low resistance 10 min   Repeat prior exercises once   Ice if stairs trigger pain
6   Gradual return   15-20 min easy walk if no worsening next day   Sit-to-stand 2 x 6; leg raises 2 x 10   Rest breaks during day
7   Assess trend   Continue flat walking only if clearly improving   Gentle repeat of best-tolerated exercises   If not improving, plan routine medical review
Safer 7-Day Habits for the Knee
- Prefer   flat surfaces   over hills or stairs.
- Keep pain during activity in the   mild range  , not escalating.
- Avoid   running, jumping, lunges, deep squats, or long stair sessions  .
- Use   supportive walking shoes  .
- When going downstairs, take   shorter steps   and use the handrail.
- If one day causes a flare, scale back the next day rather than pushing through.

For blood-pressure medication: be cautious with   over-the-counter anti-inflammatory pain medicines   such as ibuprofen or naproxen unless a clinician/pharmacist says they are appropriate, because they can interact with some blood pressure or kidney-related situations.   Acetaminophen/paracetamol   may be preferred for some people, but he should use only as directed on the label and within safe limits.
